delivery.title: Research brief: trade credit for small businesses
delivery.content:
# Trade Credit: Financing for Small Businesses

Trade credit represents a vital financing mechanism globally. Defined as allowing time to pay for goods or services—commonly net-30 terms, meaning payment due within 30 days—trade credit is the third largest funding source for U.S. small businesses.^1

## How Net-30 Trade Credit Works

When a supplier extends trade credit, a buyer receives merchandise immediately while deferring payment to an agreed date. This provides essential working capital without interest. Net-30 terms mean payment due within 30 days of invoice receipt. Late payments incur fees; on-time payments build positive trade history.^2

## Why Small Businesses Rely on Trade Credit

### Cash Flow Management

Businesses with seasonal revenue—retailers during holidays, agricultural suppliers at harvest—depend on trade credit to bridge cash flow gaps. Without supplier credit, these businesses would need bank loans or credit cards at higher interest rates.^3

### Avoiding Overdrafts

Trade credit prevents overdraft situations when receivables lag inventory purchases. A small retailer sells on net-30 credit while buying upstream on the same terms, creating a financing pipeline with minimal capital requirements.

### Building Vendor Relationships

Paying on time builds trust with suppliers, unlocking discounts or priority service during disruptions. This relationship capital helps compete against larger businesses.

## Risks of Abuse

Businesses paying late to preserve cash risk losing supplier relationships quickly. Suppliers maintain collections departments; three months of late payments typically ends credit access permanently.^2

### Impact on Credit Scores

Trade payment history feeds into business credit scores from bureaus like Dun & Bradstreet, Equifax, Experian. Poor habits damage these scores, restricting bank financing when needed most.

## Best Practices

1. Maintain spreadsheets tracking invoices and due dates
2. Set calendar reminders at 25 days for early payment
3. Build relationships with supplier finance managers for flexibility during difficulties
4. Monitor trade credit availability; disappearing supplier credit signals supply chain distress

Trade credit is trust between businesses, not bank money. Small businesses respecting these arrangements build reputation capital valuable even without formal loans.

---

^1 Source: Wikipedia article on trade credit confirms it as the third largest financing source for U.S. small businesses after bank loans and merchant credit cards. See https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trade_credit

^2 Source: Federal Reserve Bank of New York notes on trade finance discusses how trade credit terms work, noting payment discipline builds supplier relationships and affects business creditworthiness. See https://www.federalreserve.gov/econres/notes/feds-notes/tradefinance.htm

^3 Source: Investopedia's trade credit article explains how small businesses use supplier credit to manage working capital without interest-bearing debt. See https://www.investopedia.com/terms/t/trade-credit.asp
